A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Critique-Resilient Benchmarking study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments across eight models and 44 mathematics topics, including rankings, predictive validation, benchmark correlations, and human–model adjudication agreement.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds critic-reliability, answer-incompatibility, prompt-sensitivity, and capability-correlation analyses in Appendix F.

M1.justification: The feasibility gate, adversarial evaluation, adjudication procedure, self-improvement loop, and itemized bipartite Bradley–Terry model remain the same. V3 clarifies collective feasibility checking and aligns definitions with operational rules already present in v1; the prompt variants are ablations, not replacements for the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 44 mathematics topics and use AIME 2025, BRUMO 2025, and HMMT February 2025 for external validation. V3's sample questions and supplementary analyses do not introduce another dataset, domain, or substantive task requirement.

E2.justification: The original eight-model comparisons and baserate predictor in Table 2 are retained. GPT-5.4-high serves as an evaluator in new analyses, not an additional competing baseline. The GPT-5 label corrected to GPT-5.2 in Tables 4 and 7 refers to the same previously specified model.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces substantial additional evaluation protocols: GPT-5.4-high assessment of answer correctness and critique agreement/F1, and incompatibility classification of 3,779 answer pairs across 271 questions. The new prompt ablation uses two benchmarkers, seven answerers/critics excluding Gemini, and GPT-5.4-high alone instead of human adjudication. These supplement the unchanged original experimental settings.

E4.justification: V3 adds four analyses absent from v1: whether critiquing is easier than answering, whether surviving answers contradict one another, sensitivity to removing guidance or self-verification information, and correlation between answering and benchmarking strength. Appendix F and Tables 10–12 substantially expand scrutiny of the framework's assumptions and robustness.

E5.justification: The question-cluster bootstrap, fixed-hyperparameter refitting, percentile 95% intervals, and bootstrap standard errors are retained from v1 Appendix E in v3 Appendix H. Table 12 applies the existing bootstrap practice to new results; no new seed information, repeat counts, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: The original numerical results remain unchanged, but v3 adds substantial findings. Table 10 reports GPT-3.5 answer correctness of 0.157 versus critique agreement of 0.953 under the new proxy evaluator. Appendix F reports 160/3,779 incompatible answer pairs, prompt-ranking concordance W = 0.952, and answering–benchmarking correlations of rho = 0.69 and tau = 0.47. These are additional results, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Definition 3.3 replaces ill-posedness with obscurity in the answer-resilience criterion, and Definition 3.4 explicitly separates answer failures from question-invalidating ill-posedness. These substantive formal corrections align the definitions with v1's operational treatment. The Bradley–Terry equations and MAP/Laplace derivations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and principal conclusion retain the same contributions: critique-resilient evaluation beyond full human comprehension, bounded human verification, separate answering and benchmarking rankings, and stable rankings aligned with external benchmarks. The added analyses support these retained headline claims.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands the framework's rationale and interpretation. Appendix B explains the choice of two capability dimensions and obstacles to separating authoring from critiquing. Appendix F interprets the new diagnostics as evidence for verification asymmetry, prompt robustness, and fewer undetected errors with stronger models. The conclusion also reframes critic-relative correctness as enabling reuse of existing questions against stronger critics.

D1.justification: V3 supplies eight sample questions, identifies the supplementary evaluator and ablation configurations, and updates total API expenditure from approximately USD 2.3k to USD 3.3k. Original model identifiers, temperatures, hyperparameters, prompt templates, and code-access information remain available; self-improvement details move to Appendix D.

R1.justification: V3 adds Brown-Cohen et al. (2024) on doubly-efficient debate and connects it to bounded verification. Section 8 also revises the distinction from scalable oversight to emphasize evaluation and ranking rather than supervision during training or deployment. The broader related-work coverage remains intact.

P1.justification: V3 shortens the title, adds a conflict-of-interest disclosure, makes localized explanatory edits, and moves self-improvement and retry details into the appendix. New appendices organize model-choice discussion, sample questions, and additional analyses, while most existing prose and the main section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 adds the protocol flowchart as Figure 1 and three analysis tables, Tables 10–12. Existing charts, interface screenshots, and prompt figures are retained with renumbering, relocation, and some resizing; the document's basic visual structure remains similar.

improvement.justification: V3 makes the formal outcome definitions consistent with the operational protocol and adds useful evidence about prompt sensitivity and surviving-answer consistency that v1 lacked. The flowchart and model-choice discussion also improve clarity. The gains are bounded: several new diagnostics rely on GPT-5.4-high as a correctness proxy, and low mutual incompatibility does not establish a low absolute error rate or demonstrate that stronger critics cause fewer errors. The original main empirical evidence remains unchanged.
